name: Search the literature on OpenAlex
summary: Free, key-less API over ~250M works: find papers by topic, author, venue or concept, with citation counts and open-access links.
commands: curl -s 'https://api.openalex.org/works?search=post-quantum+cryptography+masking&per-page=25&mailto=YOUR_EMAIL' | jq -r '.results[] | "\(.publication_year)\t\(.cited_by_count)\t\(.title)\t\(.doi)"'
curl -s 'https://api.openalex.org/works?filter=title.search:masked+kyber,from_publication_date:2020-01-01&per-page=50&mailto=YOUR_EMAIL'
outputs: A JSON list of works with title, year, DOI, venue and cited_by_count
prompt: Start here: it needs no key and covers everything Crossref indexes plus citation graph. Put a real contact email in mailto= for the polite pool. Record what you found in references/, with what each source is used for — never paste a raw result list into the manuscript, and never cite a paper from its abstract alone.

name: Follow the citation graph on Semantic Scholar
summary: Graph API for references, citations and influential citations of a known paper — the fastest way to find what a key paper missed and who answered it.
commands: curl -s 'https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/DOI:10.1109/TII.2020.1234567?fields=title,year,citationCount,references.title,references.year,references.externalIds'
curl -s 'https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/DOI:<doi>/citations?fields=title,year,venue,isInfluential&limit=100'
outputs: JSON with the paper's references and citing works
prompt: Use it for backward and forward snowballing from the two or three papers that anchor the related-work section. Unauthenticated calls are rate-limited: batch them and pause on HTTP 429. An API key raises the limit and belongs in the environment, never in this file.

name: Search arXiv for preprints
summary: Query the arXiv API for preprints, which is where security, ML and systems work appears a year before the journal version.
commands: curl -s 'https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=all:%22masked+kyber%22&sortBy=submittedDate&sortOrder=descending&max_results=25'
outputs: An Atom feed of matching preprints with abstract, authors and submission date
prompt: A preprint is citable but not peer-reviewed: say so in the text when it matters, and check whether a peer-reviewed version now exists before citing the eprint. For cryptography, also check the IACR ePrint archive (eprint.iacr.org), which arXiv does not index.

name: Look a work up on Crossref
summary: Authoritative publisher metadata by DOI or title: authors, pages, volume, issue and year — the source of truth for a reference entry.
commands: curl -s 'https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Energy+aware+post-quantum+automotive&rows=5&mailto=YOUR_EMAIL' | jq '.message.items[] | {title,DOI,issued,page,container_title}'
curl -sLH 'Accept: application/x-bibtex' 'https://doi.org/10.1109/TII.2020.1234567'
outputs: JSON metadata, or a ready-to-paste BibTeX entry from the second command
prompt: The second command is content negotiation: it returns the publisher's own BibTeX for a DOI. Prefer it to hand-typing an entry. Publisher BibTeX is often mis-capitalised and over-abbreviated — fix the title case and the venue name, but never change an author list or a page range to make it look tidier.

name: Search a paywalled database in a browser session
summary: IEEE Xplore, ACM DL, ScienceDirect, Scopus and Web of Science need institutional access and block scripted clients; drive them from a real browser session instead.
commands: # Open a persistent, anti-detection browser session and search from there.
# Google Scholar and Elsevier block plain curl and most headless browsers outright.
outputs: Search results read from the page; PDFs saved under sources/ when licence allows
risks: Scripted access can breach a publisher's terms and get the institution's IP range blocked — search interactively, at human pace, and never bulk-download
prompt: Reach for this only when the open sources above do not have the work. Respect the licence: a PDF saved under sources/ is for reading, and it is never redistributed with the artifact. Record in references/ what the source supports, not the PDF itself.

name: Verify every bibliography entry against its DOI
summary: Check each .bib entry's authors, year, venue and pages against Crossref before submission, and flag the ones that cannot be resolved.
commands: grep -n '^@' References.bib | wc -l
# For each DOI in the file, fetch Crossref metadata and diff the fields that matter.
outputs: A list of entries that differ from the publisher record, or that have no DOI
prompt: BibTeX has no comment character inside an entry: a `% CHECK` on the same line as a field silently corrupts it, usually surfacing as an 'empty author' warning in the .blg. Put any marker on its own line before the `@`. Standards bodies (ISO, FIPS, AUTOSAR) legitimately have no author — those warnings are expected, and the fix is a `@misc` with an explicit `author = {{ISO}}`.

name: Sync with Overleaf over the Git bridge
summary: Pull co-author edits from Overleaf and push local ones, when the account has the Git bridge (paid plans only).
commands: git remote add overleaf https://git.overleaf.com/<project-id>
git fetch overleaf && git merge overleaf/master
git push overleaf HEAD:master
outputs: A merge with the co-authors' commits, or a clean push
risks: A force-push replaces work a co-author did in the browser, with no undo on their side
prompt: Always fetch and merge before pushing. The credential is an Overleaf Git token: it lives in the environment or a local .env that is never committed, and it never appears in this memory. On a free account the bridge does not exist — use the browser-session skill instead.

name: Work with Overleaf without the Git bridge
summary: Read and update an Overleaf project from a logged-in browser session when the account has no Git bridge.
commands: # Open the saved, logged-in browser session for Overleaf and work through the project UI.
outputs: The project's file list and contents; an uploaded revision
risks: Replacing a file wipes whatever a co-author typed since your last read — Overleaf keeps history, but the merge is yours to redo by hand
prompt: Read the project's update history BEFORE writing anything, and fold any co-author edit into your version first. Rebase onto their work; never overwrite it. Treat every upload as destructive and confirm with a human. The session credential stays in the browser profile and never enters this memory.

name: Build the manuscript PDF
summary: Compile the manuscript with the bibliography resolved, and read the log rather than the PDF for problems.
commands: latexmk -pdf main.tex
# or, where a Makefile exists: make
pdfinfo main.pdf | grep Pages
outputs: main.pdf, and a .log whose last lines name every unresolved reference and overfull box
prompt: A build that produces a PDF is not a build that succeeded: grep the .log for 'Warning: Citation', 'undefined' and 'Overfull' before saying it is clean. Check the page count against the venue's limit on every build — a paper that is over the limit is desk-rejected, and the fix is never a last-day font change.

name: Export figures as vector art
summary: Produce figures the publisher will accept: vector, sized to one or two columns, legible in greyscale.
commands: # Export PDF or EPS from the plotting tool, not PNG.
pdffonts figure.pdf   # every font must be embedded
outputs: A vector figure whose fonts are embedded and whose text is at least 7pt at final size
prompt: Size the figure to its final width (one column or two) before choosing font sizes — scaling a figure down afterwards is what makes axis labels unreadable. Never encode meaning in colour alone: the paper will be printed in greyscale and read by people who cannot distinguish the hues.

name: Assemble the submission package
summary: Produce exactly what the venue asks for: the PDF, the sources, the figures, and nothing that breaks anonymity.
commands: # Build clean from a fresh checkout, then collect the files the venue lists.
grep -ril '<author name>\|<institution>\|github.com/<org>' . # anonymity sweep
outputs: An archive matching the venue's file list, built from a clean tree
risks: Submission is irreversible and often one-shot per deadline
PDF metadata and figure files carry author names even when the text does not
prompt: Never submit without a human. Build from a clean checkout so no local placeholder survives. Under an anonymous regime, sweep the PDF metadata, the figure files and every URL — the acknowledgements and the funding statement are where anonymity usually breaks.

name: Look up a venue or an author on DBLP
summary: DBLP is the bibliography of record for computer science: complete venue listings, disambiguated authors, and clean BibTeX.
commands: curl -s 'https://dblp.org/search/publ/api?q=masked+kyber&format=json&h=30' | jq -r '.result.hits.hit[].info | "\(.year)\t\(.venue)\t\(.title)"'
curl -s 'https://dblp.org/search/author/api?q=<surname>&format=json'
# Every DBLP entry has a .bib URL: append .bib?param=1 to the record page
outputs: JSON hits with year, venue, title and a stable DBLP key
prompt: For a CS paper this is usually better than Crossref for BibTeX: the venue names are consistent, the author disambiguation is curated by humans, and conference proceedings are complete. Use it to check you have not missed the obvious paper from the venue you are submitting to — reviewers come from there.

name: Search PubMed and Europe PMC
summary: The life-sciences literature, with full-text search over open-access content in Europe PMC.
commands: curl -s 'https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=<query>&retmax=50&retmode=json'
curl -s 'https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=<query>&format=json&pageSize=50'
outputs: PMIDs from PubMed; full records including open-access full text from Europe PMC
prompt: Europe PMC searches full text, PubMed searches abstracts and MeSH terms — they answer different questions, so run both. If the paper is a systematic review, the exact query string and the date you ran it are part of the method and belong in the manuscript: record them in references/ as you go, not afterwards.

name: Search the domain's preprint server
summary: The server your field actually reads: IACR ePrint for cryptography, bioRxiv/medRxiv for life sciences, SSRN for law and economics, RePEc for economics, HAL for French institutions.
commands: # IACR ePrint (cryptography): https://eprint.iacr.org/search?q=<query>
curl -s 'https://api.biorxiv.org/details/biorxiv/10.1101/<doi-suffix>'
# SSRN, RePEc and HAL each have their own search; arXiv is a separate skill
outputs: Preprints your field treats as citable, which arXiv often does not index
prompt: Missing the preprint server of your own field is how a paper gets a reviewer saying 'this was solved last year'. In cryptography, IACR ePrint is where the work appears first and is routinely cited — arXiv is not a substitute. Always check whether a published version exists before citing the preprint, and say which one you are citing.

name: Find a legal full text for a paywalled paper
summary: Unpaywall and OpenAlex know where an open-access copy of a DOI lives, including author manuscripts in institutional repositories.
commands: curl -s 'https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/<doi>?email=YOUR_EMAIL' | jq '.best_oa_location.url_for_pdf'
curl -s 'https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:<doi>?mailto=YOUR_EMAIL' | jq '.best_oa_location'
outputs: A URL to a legally hosted copy, or null when there is none
prompt: Try this before the institutional login and long before anything else: most papers have an author manuscript in a repository, and it is the same text. If there is no open copy, use the institutional route — never a shadow library. A null answer is a real answer.

name: Run and log a systematic search
summary: A reproducible search: one written query per database, the date, the hit counts, the deduplication, and the screening decisions.
triggers: how did you find these papers
commands: # Run the same query against each database, saving raw results per source.
# Deduplicate by DOI, then by normalised title.
# Record counts at every stage: identified, deduplicated, screened, included.
outputs: A search log with per-database queries, dates and counts, and a numbered list of included works
prompt: In a survey or systematic review the search IS the method, and an unrecorded search cannot be defended or repeated. Write the query string down before running it. Record exclusions with a reason, not silently. The counts at each stage are what a PRISMA-style flow diagram is made of — see the literature-search playbook.

name: Audit every claim against its evidence
summary: Walk the manuscript sentence by sentence and check that each assertion is either supported by a named result, attributed to a citation, or marked as a hypothesis.
triggers: does the abstract match the results
commands: # For each file in claims/, find where the manuscript states it and what it cites as support.
# Then the reverse sweep: for each strong sentence in the manuscript, find the claim file behind it.
outputs: A list of assertions with no named evidence, and of claims stated more strongly in the abstract than in the results
prompt: The two failures this catches are different. One: a sentence in the paper that no result supports. Two: a claim that IS supported, but stated at one strength in §VI and a stronger one in the abstract — that is the most common reviewer complaint and the easiest to fix before submission. Report both as a list with file and line; do not rewrite the sentences without a human, because softening a claim is an authorial decision, not an editorial one.

name: Trace every number in the text back to the data
summary: Regenerate the tables and figures from the raw data and diff them against what the manuscript prints, so no number survives from an older run.
commands: # Rerun the analysis from the raw data into the generated table/figure files.
# Diff the regenerated outputs against what is committed, and against what the PDF shows.
outputs: A clean diff, or a list of numbers in the manuscript that no current run produces
prompt: A number that no script reproduces is a number nobody can defend. This is the check that catches the classic failure: the analysis was rerun, the figure was updated, and one value in the prose was not. Run it before every submission and after every change to the data. If a value cannot be traced, say so — do not adjust it to match.

name: Recompute the reported statistics
summary: Check that reported test statistics, degrees of freedom, p-values, effect sizes and confidence intervals are mutually consistent.
commands: # Extract every reported test: statistic, df, p, n, effect size, CI.
# Recompute p from the statistic and df, and the CI from the effect size and its standard error.
# Flag any mismatch beyond rounding.
outputs: A table of reported vs recomputed values, with the mismatches flagged
prompt: Inconsistent statistics are found by reviewers and by automated screening at many journals, and they are usually transcription errors rather than misconduct — which is exactly why catching them yourself is cheap and not catching them is expensive. Check also that n is the same everywhere it appears, that the test matches the design, and that a significant result has an effect size reported next to it.

name: Check each citation supports the sentence it is attached to
summary: Verify that the cited work actually says what the sentence claims it says, rather than being topically adjacent.
commands: # For each \cite in the manuscript, read the sentence and the cited work's actual claim.
# Flag: citation used for a stronger claim than the source makes; citation of a survey for a primary result; citation inherited from another paper's reference list without reading.
outputs: A list of citations whose source does not support the sentence as written
prompt: Citation drift is the failure mode where a claim gets stronger each time it is re-cited, until it is attributed to a paper that never made it. The tell is a citation you inherited from someone else's related-work section. Never confirm a citation from its abstract alone — the assumptions and the threat model are what you are citing it for, and they are not in the abstract.

name: Sweep the threats to validity
summary: Work through internal, external, construct and conclusion validity against the actual design, and check each real threat is stated in the paper.
commands: # Internal: what else could have caused the effect? Confounds, order effects, drift, selection.
# External: what does the result NOT transfer to? One platform, one dataset, one population.
# Construct: does the metric measure what it is named after?
# Conclusion: is the statistical inference warranted by n and the spread?
outputs: A list of threats, each either addressed by the design or stated in the paper as a limitation
prompt: A threat that the design cannot remove must appear in the paper. Reviewers do not punish a stated limitation; they punish a hidden one, and they find it. The most common miss is construct validity — a metric whose name promises more than it measures. Never soften a real threat into a strength.

name: Review the draft as a hostile reviewer
summary: A deliberate attack pass on the paper's own argument, producing the objections a real reviewer would raise, with the strongest ones first.
commands: # Read the paper as a reviewer who wants to reject it and must justify the rejection.
outputs: A numbered list of objections, each with what would answer it: new evidence, a softer claim, or a stated limitation
prompt: Be specific and be harsh: 'the baseline is unfair because X' beats 'the evaluation could be stronger'. Attack in this order — the contribution (is it a contribution?), the claim-evidence gap, the baseline, the metric, the statistics, external validity, then the writing. For each objection say which of three things fixes it: more evidence, a weaker claim, or an admitted limitation. Record the round in reviews/ so the same objection is not rediscovered twice, and so the answers survive into the rebuttal.

risks: A paper repository must start private and stay private: a public repository before acceptance can break a venue's anonymity requirement, breach a publisher's embargo, or redistribute a dataset you do not own
name: Create the article's repository
summary: Put the manuscript, data and memory in a private Git repository, so the work survives the machine and the co-authors can clone it.
commands: git init -b main && git add -A && git commit -m 'chore: track the manuscript'
gh repo create <org>/<name> --private --source=. --remote=origin --push
outputs: A private remote with the manuscript and its memory pushed
prompt: Private, always, and let a human decide when that changes. Before the first push, check what is being committed: build artifacts, downloaded PDFs from publishers, raw data under a licence that forbids redistribution, and any .env. A paper repository is also the thing that makes drift detection work at all — without it, the memory cannot be compared against anything.

risks: A single missed name, path or commit author de-anonymises the submission, and that cannot be undone once reviewers have seen it
name: Publish an anonymised copy of the artifact
summary: Under double-anonymous review, give reviewers the code and data without giving them the authors.
commands: # Export a clean copy with no git history, no author names, no institutional paths.
git log --format='%an %ae' | sort -u   # who appears in the history you are about to strip
grep -ril '<surname>\|<institution>\|<funder>' .   # sweep before publishing
outputs: An anonymised copy whose content carries no author identity
prompt: Git history, file paths, PDF metadata, figure source files, package names, README acknowledgements and licence headers all carry identity. Export, strip and re-check; never just flip a repository to public. Ask the venue what it accepts — some require a specific anonymising service, and a bare public repo may be a desk reject on its own.

name: Tag the exact version that was submitted
summary: Tag and archive the submitted PDF and sources, so the next revision has a baseline to diff against.
commands: git tag -a submitted-<venue>-<yyyy-mm-dd> -m 'as submitted'
git push origin --tags
cp paper/main.pdf paper/.rev/submitted-<venue>-<yyyy-mm-dd>.pdf
outputs: An annotated tag and an archived PDF of exactly what the venue received
prompt: Do this the day you submit, not when the reviews arrive. Without it, the revision cannot produce a reliable diff, and the editor's request for 'a marked-up version showing the changes' becomes guesswork. Record in the memory which tag corresponds to which submission.

name: Produce the marked-up revision
summary: Generate the change-marked PDF that editors ask for with a revision, from the submitted tag to the current draft.
commands: git show submitted-<venue>-<date>:paper/main.tex > /tmp/old.tex
latexdiff /tmp/old.tex paper/main.tex > paper/diff.tex
cd paper && pdflatex diff.tex
outputs: A PDF with additions and deletions marked
prompt: latexdiff chokes on changed table and figure environments; when it does, mark those sections by hand rather than shipping a broken diff. Check the diff PDF compiles and is readable before sending it — an unreadable markup annoys exactly the person deciding your paper's fate.

risks: Publishing a deposit is irreversible: the files and the DOI are permanent and public
Publishing a deposit that names the authors breaks anonymity at a double-anonymous venue
Uploading data you do not own redistributes it under your name
name: Deposit the artifact on Zenodo and mint a DOI
summary: Create a Zenodo deposit, reserve its DOI so the manuscript can cite it, upload the files, and publish only when a human says so.
commands: curl -s -X POST 'https://zenodo.org/api/deposit/depositions' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "Authorization: Bearer $ZENODO_TOKEN" -d '{}'
# Reserve the DOI before submission: set metadata.prereserve_doi = true, then read metadata.prereserve_doi.doi
curl -s -X PUT '<bucket_url>/<filename>' -H "Authorization: Bearer $ZENODO_TOKEN" --upload-file <file>
# Publishing is a separate, irreversible call — do not make it without a human
outputs: A deposit with a reserved DOI, and after publication a DOI that resolves permanently
prompt: The reserved DOI is the point: it lets the manuscript cite the artifact before the artifact is public, which is what the data availability statement needs. Keep the deposit unpublished until the paper is accepted, or use the venue's anonymised route. The token lives in the environment and never enters this memory. Check every file's licence before uploading, and give the deposit the same author list and title as the paper.

risks: A preprint cannot be deleted, only withdrawn or superseded — the original stays visible
Posting during double-anonymous review breaches many venues' policies
Posting a version whose numbers later change leaves the wrong numbers permanently citable
name: Post the preprint
summary: Put the manuscript on arXiv, IACR ePrint or the field's server, after checking the venue allows it.
commands: # Check the venue's preprint policy FIRST, then submit through the server's own interface.
outputs: A public preprint with a permanent identifier
prompt: Ask a human, and check the venue's policy before anything else: some journals treat a preprint as prior publication and some anonymous venues forbid it during review. Never post a draft with unresolved placeholders — the preprint is the version the world will cite. Record the preprint identifier in the memory so later versions can be linked to it.

name: Check the length against the venue's limit
summary: Count pages and words per section, so trimming is aimed at the section that is actually over budget.
commands: pdfinfo main.pdf | grep Pages
texcount -inc -sum main.tex
texcount -inc -sub=section main.tex
outputs: Total pages, and a word count per section
prompt: Measure before cutting. The section that feels long is rarely the one over budget, and the usual answer — shrinking figures or fonts — is both visible to reviewers and often against the venue's rules. Compare the per-section word counts against a published paper from the same venue: that comparison tells you which section is out of proportion.

name: Run a language pass over the manuscript
summary: Spelling, consistency and register, on the text only, without the agent silently rewriting the argument.
commands: aspell --mode=tex --lang=en list < main.tex | sort -u
# Consistency: one spelling of each technical term, one tense per section, one notation per symbol
outputs: A list of suspected spellings and inconsistencies, for a human to accept or reject
prompt: Report, do not rewrite. A language pass that edits sentences silently changes claims — 'may reduce' becoming 'reduces' is a spelling-level edit with a scientific meaning. List what you would change and let the author choose. Check notation consistency while you are there: the same symbol meaning two things is worse than any typo.

name: Assemble the response to reviewers
summary: Turn the reviewers' reports into a point-by-point response where every point names what actually changed in the manuscript.
commands: # One file per review round in reviews/: quote each point verbatim, number it, answer it.
# Cross-reference each answer to the section and line that changed.
outputs: A numbered response where each point cites the change that answers it
prompt: Quote the reviewer verbatim; paraphrasing a criticism to make it easier to answer is the fastest way to lose a referee. Every point gets one of three honest answers: we changed X (say where), we disagree and here is why, or we agree and cannot fix it in this paper (say so as a limitation). A point answered with no change to the manuscript must say that explicitly. Record the round in reviews/ so the next revision knows what was already promised.
